1. Core Clinical Tension: A 48-year-old immunocompetent male from Eastern India presented with an acute peritonitis from small-bowel perforation superimposed on a 1-month prodrome of fever, cough, weight loss, and apical pulmonary infiltrates. Because of its notorious ability to mimic pulmonary and abdominal tuberculosis or typhoidal perforation ('the great mimicker'), he had been inappropriately placed on empiric anti-tuberculous therapy before microbiological identification revealed an environmental saprophyte.

2. Admission Breakpoint: Admission triage terminates after the evaluation of acute peritonitis, admission hematology and chemistry labs, chest radiography, erect abdominal radiograph confirming subdiaphragmatic pneumoperitoneum, and abdominal ultrasonography. Exploratory laparotomy, peritoneal pus sampling, Gram staining, and bacterial culture constitute the post-triage confirmatory stage.

3. Differential Distinctions: Intestinal tuberculosis with perforation was strongly favored initially based on the chronic pulmonary apical infiltrates and endemic setting, but sputum acid-fast stains were negative. Typhoid enteritis with ileal perforation and perforated peptic ulcer were excluded by peritoneal pus analysis revealing characteristic bipolar 'safety-pin' Gram-negative bacilli and culture growth of Burkholderia pseudomallei, confirming disseminated melioidosis.
case_prompt:
A 48-year-old man residing in West Bengal, India, presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe generalized abdominal pain and distension of 2 hours' duration. For the preceding month, he had experienced low-grade fevers, a cough productive of scanty sputum, and an unintentional 3-kg weight loss. Because of this subacute respiratory presentation and bilateral upper-zone pulmonary opacities noted on chest radiography at an outside health center, he had been empirically prescribed an outpatient regimen for presumed chronic granulomatous pulmonary infection, despite negative initial sputum microscopic smears on two separate evaluations.

On physical examination, the patient was in severe distress, tachycardic, and tachypneic. Heart rate was 112 beats per minute, blood pressure was 134/86 mmHg, respiratory rate was 36 breaths per minute, and temperature was 37.8°C (100°F). The abdomen was markedly distended, diffusely rigid, and exquisitely tender with involuntary muscular guarding and rebound tenderness that worsened with cough or movement. Abdominal percussion yielded diffuse tympany throughout. Chest auscultation revealed diminished vesicular breath sounds and coarse crackles over both infraclavicular regions.

Admission laboratory investigations revealed a hemoglobin level of 110 g/L, total leukocyte count of 11.2 x 10⁹/L (68% neutrophils, 27% lymphocytes), and polymorphonuclear leukocytosis on peripheral smear without blasts or parasites. Liver enzymes showed aspartate aminotransferase of 64 U/L, alanine aminotransferase of 78 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase of 156 U/L. Basic metabolic parameters showed blood urea nitrogen of 12 mmol/L, serum creatinine of 1.1 mg/dL, sodium of 134 mEq/L, and potassium of 3.4 mEq/L. Random blood glucose was 98 mg/dL. Serum amylase, serum lipase, and urinalysis were normal. Serologic tests for hepatitis B surface antigen, hepatitis C virus, and human immunodeficiency virus were non-reactive.

An erect plain radiograph of the abdomen demonstrated bilateral free air under the diaphragmatic domes. A concurrent chest radiograph confirmed bilateral upper-zone pulmonary infiltrates with prominent bronchovascular markings. Abdominal ultrasonography showed marked intraperitoneal gas and free fluid with internal echogenicity throughout the peritoneal cavity.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pulmonary and Intestinal Tuberculosis with Ileal Perforation
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A 1-month history of fever, cough, weight loss, apical lung consolidation, and ileal perforation strongly suggested gastrointestinal tuberculosis; however, repeated sputum smears were negative, and peritoneal fluid failed to demonstrate acid-fast bacilli, growing Gram-negative bacilli instead.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: With this clinical picture and bilateral upper zone opacities in X-ray chest [Figure 1], the patient was put on anti-tubercular therapy in another center (Directly Observed Treatment Shortcourse-Category I) though the sputum was negative for acid fast bacilli on Ziehl-Neelson stain on two occasions.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Typhoid Enteritis (Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi) with Ileal Perforation
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Acute distal ileal perforation occurring after an indolent febrile prodrome in an endemic Indian setting is classic for Salmonella enterica infection; however, the associated chronic apical lung cavitation, resistance to standard empiric cephalosporins, and growth of wrinkled non-enteric colonies excluded typhoid fever.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: On opening the abdomen, we found around 500 ml of purulent fluid and two small perforations 1cm apart about 20 cm proximal to the ileocaecal junction.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Urgent laparotomy demonstrated purulent peritonitis secondary to two small ileal perforations; microscopic analysis of the peritoneal pus revealed Gram-negative bacilli with classic bipolar ('safety-pin') staining, and culture yielded characteristic dry, wrinkled colonies on MacConkey and blood agar confirmed by biochemical profiling as Burkholderia pseudomallei, establishing disseminated melioidosis presenting as an acute surgical abdomen.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Gram staining of the pus showed Gram-negative bacilli with bipolar staining. The pus culture showed lactose fermenting pink colonies in MacConkey's agar on 2nd day which turned dry and wrinkled on day 4. The blood agar showed dry and wrinkled colonies on day 4 suspicious of B. pseudomallei [Figure 2].

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case following Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Admission presentation strictly incorporates triage examination, laboratory values, erect abdominal X-ray pneumoperitoneum, and ultrasound free fluid while withholding laparotomy findings, pus Gram stain, and bacterial culture.
